newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke rejects rate rise call ahead of BOE report.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke rejects rate rise call ahead of BOE report.

text.p: British Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke pre-empted what is likely to be a tough warning on inflation from the Bank of England on Wednesday by rejecting the central bank's call for higher interest rates.
Clarke told a radio interviewer that the strong British pound was having a big deflationary effect on the British economy and said he saw no need for tighter credit.
Although Clarke has said the Bank of England is wrong to push for higher interest rates, he sought to play down the extent of any disagreement between the government and the Bank.
"I am disagreeing with him (Bank of England Governor Eddie Goerge) over one quarter of one percent on interest rates," Clarke said.

The Bank of England is expected to renew its warnings about an increase in inflationary pressure in Britain and to repeat its calls for a rate increase when it issues is quarterly inflation report at 1130 GMT on Wednesday.
Ahead of the report, the central bank's deputy governor Howard Davies said a modest rate rise was needed to make sure the government met its 2.5 percent inflation target.
The underlying inflation rate is stuck above target, but it eased to 3.1 percent in December from November's 3.3 percent.
Davies told a conference on Tuesday the Bank was seeking a quarter point increase above the current six percent bank base rate now and "perhaps a little more later in the year".
The government is eager not to have to increase interest rates ahead of a general election which must be held by May 22.

Clarke pointed to strong growth in the British economy and also said a report out later today, which is expected to show another strong fall in unemployment, indicated that the jobs market was moving in the right direction.
The economy had been moving ahead steadily since Christmas and not shown any sign of speeding up. "I think it is not yet at the stage where I have to put the brakes on," he said.
The government has argued that the strong pound is depressing prices. Sterling has hit a new 52-month high against the mark of 2.76.
Britain last raised interest rates by a quarter point to 6.0 percent on October 30 last year.

Earlier on Wednesday a British tabloid newspaper, The Daily Mirror, said British unemployment had fallen by 57,800 in January, way above market forecasts of a 30,000 decline. Unemployment fell to a six year low of 1.88 million in December.
Official employment data will be published at 0930 GMT.
